a: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright, poet, and actor widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, he likely attended the local grammar school where he studied Latin classics, though no university records exist. He married Anne Hathaway at 18 and later moved to London, where he became a shareholder and principal playwright of the Lord Chamberlain's Men (later the King's Men). His enduring fame rests on 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and several narrative poems that explore the full breadth of human experience with unmatched psychological insight and linguistic creativity.

a: Shakespeare's Hamlet (c. 1600) follows Prince Hamlet of Denmark, who is visited by his father's ghost and commanded to avenge his murder by Claudius, the king's brother who has seized the throne and married Hamlet's mother. The play delves into profound questions about life, death, madness, betrayal, and the nature of action through Hamlet's philosophical soliloquies, most famously 'To be or not to be.' Its psychological complexity, rich symbolism, and exploration of human frailty have made it one of the most analyzed and performed works in world literature.

a: Romeo and Juliet (c. 1595) tells the story of two young lovers from feuding families in Verona whose passionate romance ends in tragic death. The play explores the destructive power of hatred, the intensity of youthful love, and the role of fate and societal expectations in human affairs. Its iconic scenes — the balcony encounter, the duel between Tybalt and Mercutio, and the heartbreaking final moments in the tomb — have become archetypal symbols of doomed love.

a: Macbeth (c. 1606) is Shakespeare's shortest and most intense tragedy, following a Scottish general whose ambition, stoked by three witches and his ruthless wife, drives him to murder King Duncan and seize the throne. The play vividly portrays the psychological unraveling of its protagonist as guilt, paranoia, and violence consume him and Lady Macbeth. Its themes of unchecked ambition, the corrupting nature of power, and the relationship between fate and free will are underscored by some of Shakespeare's most memorable lines and imagery.

a: Shakespeare revolutionized English drama by developing complex characters with psychological depth, blending comedy and tragedy in ways that defied classical conventions, and elevating the soliloquy into a tool for profound introspection. He expanded the English lexicon by coining or popularizing over 1,700 words and countless phrases still in use today. His plays were performed at the Globe Theatre, a circular open-air playhouse on the Thames that he co-owned, which featured minimal sets but relied on powerful language and audience imagination. Shakespeare's influence pervades modern literature, film, psychology, and everyday speech, making him a foundational figure in Western culture.

Why are Shakespeare's sonnets considered important?
a: Shakespeare wrote 154 sonnets, a sequence that explores love, beauty, mortality, jealousy, and the passage of time through a distinctive 14-line structure with three quatrains and a concluding couplet (ababcdcdefefgg). The first 126 sonnets address a handsome young man, urging him to marry and procreate, while the later sonnets shift to a complex and passionate relationship with a mysterious 'dark lady.' These poems are celebrated for their emotional intensity, linguistic virtuosity, and their deep meditation on whether art can confer immortality upon beauty and love.
